danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Der gik lang tid, før Pierre kunne falde i søvn den nat. Han vandrede frem og tilbage i sit værelse, snart fordybet i et vanskeligt problem med rynket pande, snart pludselig trækkende på skuldrene og krympende sig, og snart smilende lykkeligt.

Han tænkte på fyrst Andrej, på Natasja og på deres kærlighed, det ene øjeblik skinsyg på hendes fortid, det næste bebrejdende sig selv for den følelse. Klokken var allerede seks om morgenen, og han gik stadig frem og tilbage.

»Nå, hvad kan man gøre, når det ikke kan undgås? Hvad kan man gøre? Det må tydeligvis være sådan,« sagde han til sig selv, og efter hastigt at have klædt sig af gik han i seng, lykkelig og ophidset, men fri for tøven og ubeslutsomhed.
»Hvor mærkelig og umulig en sådan lykke end forekommer, må jeg gøre alt for, at hun og jeg kan blive mand og hustru,« sagde han til sig selv.
Et par dage forinden havde Pierre besluttet at rejse til Petersborg om fredagen. Da han vågnede om torsdagen, kom Savjelitj for at spørge ham om pakningen til rejsen.

»Hvad, til Petersborg? Hvad er Petersborg? Hvem er der i Petersborg?« spurgte han uvilkårligt, skønt kun til sig selv. »Åh ja, for længe siden, inden alt dette skete, agtede jeg af en eller anden grund at rejse til Petersborg,« tænkte han. »Hvorfor? Men måske tager jeg af sted. Sikke en god fyr han er, og hvor opmærksom, og hvor han husker alt,« tænkte han og betragtede Savjelitjs gamle ansigt, »og sikke et behageligt smil!«
»Nå, Savjelitj, vil du stadig ikke modtage din frihed?« spurgte Pierre ham.
»Hvad skal jeg med frihed, Deres Excellence? Vi levede under den afdøde greve — Guds rige være hans! — og vi har levet under Dem også, uden nogensinde at lide uret.«
»Og dine børn?«
»Børnene klarer sig lige så godt. Med sådanne herrer kan man leve.«
»Men hvad med mine arvinger?« sagde Pierre. »Hvis jeg nu pludselig gifter mig... det kunne jo ske,« tilføjede han med et ufrivilligt smil.
»Hvis jeg tør sige det, Deres Excellence, så ville det være en god ting.«
»Hvor let han tager det,« tænkte Pierre. »Han aner ikke, hvor frygteligt og farligt det er. For tidligt eller for sent... det er forfærdeligt!«
»Så hvad er Deres ordrer? Rejser De i morgen?« spurgte Savjelitj.

»Nej, jeg udsætter det lidt. Jeg siger til senere. Du må tilgive det besvær, jeg har påført dig,« sagde Pierre, og da han så Savjelitjs smil, tænkte han: »Men hvor mærkeligt det er, at han ikke ved, at nu findes der intet Petersborg for mig, og at det må afgøres først af alt! Men sandsynligvis ved han det godt og lader bare som om. Skal jeg tale med ham om det? Hvad mon han mener?« tænkte Pierre. »Nej, en anden gang....«
Ved frokosten fortalte Pierre sin kusine, fyrstinden, at han havde besøgt fyrstinde Marja dagen før og dér havde truffet — »Hvem tror De? Natasja Rostova!«
Fyrstinden syntes ikke at se noget mere usædvanligt heri, end hvis han havde set Anna Semjonovna.
»Kender De hende?« spurgte Pierre.
»Jeg har set fyrstinden,« svarede hun. »Jeg har hørt, at de arrangerer et parti for hende med den unge Rostov. Det ville være godt for familien Rostov, de siges at være fuldstændig ruinerede.«
»Nej, jeg mener — kender De Natasja Rostova?«
»Jeg hørte om den affære dengang. Det var meget beklageligt.«
»Nej, hun forstår det enten ikke, eller hun lader som ingenting,« tænkte Pierre. »Bedre ikke at sige noget til hende heller.«
Fyrstinden havde også forberedt proviant til Pierres rejse.
»Hvor er de alle venlige,« tænkte Pierre. »Hvad er det mærkelige, at de bekymrer sig om disse ting nu, hvor det ikke længere kan interessere dem. Og alt sammen for min skyld!«
Samme dag kom politichefen til Pierre og inviterede ham til at sende en repræsentant til det Facetterede Palads for at afhente ting, der skulle tilbageleveres til deres ejere den dag.

»Og denne mand også,« tænkte Pierre og betragtede politichefens ansigt. »Sikke en fin, flot mand, og hvor venlig. At bekymre sig om sådanne småting nu! Og de siger, at han ikke er ærlig og tager imod bestikkelse. Sikke noget sludder! Og i øvrigt, hvorfor skulle han ikke tage imod bestikkelse? Det er den måde, han er opdraget på. Alle gør det. Men sikke et behageligt, godt ansigt, og hvor han smiler.«
Pierre tog til middag hos fyrstinde Marja.

Da han kørte gennem gaderne forbi de nedbrændte huse, blev han overrasket over skønheden i disse ruiner. De maleriske skorstenspiber og nedstyrtede mure i de udbrændte kvarterer, der strakte sig ud og skjulte hinanden, mindede ham om Rhinen og Colosseum. Kuskene, han mødte, og folkene i deres vogne, tømrerne, der med økser huggede bjælker til de nye huse, torvekonerne og de handlende, alle så de på ham med fornøjede, strålende øjne, der syntes at sige: »Nå, dér har vi ham! Lad os se, hvad der kommer ud af det!«

Foran indgangen til fyrstinde Marjas hus blev Pierre grebet af tvivl, om han virkelig havde været der aftenen før og virkelig set Natasja og talt med hende. »Måske bildte jeg mig det ind; måske går jeg ind og finder ingen.« Men næppe var han trådt ind i rummet, før han mærkede hendes nærhed med hele sit væsen ved et pludseligt tab af frihed. Hun bar den samme sorte kjole med bløde folder og havde håret sat på samme måde som aftenen før, men var i øvrigt helt anderledes.

Hun var, som han havde kendt hende næsten som barn og siden som fyrst Andrejs forlovede. Et lyst, spørgende skær lyste i hendes øjne, og i hendes ansigt var der et venligt og mærkeligt gavtyveagtigt udtryk.
Pierre spiste hos dem og ville have tilbragt hele aftenen dér, men fyrstinde Marja skulle til vesper, og Pierre forlod huset med hende.

Næste dag kom han tidligt, spiste og blev hele aftenen. Skønt fyrstinde Marja og Natasja tydeligvis var glade for at se deres gæst, og skønt al Pierres interesse nu var samlet om dette hus, havde de hen på aftenen talt om alting, og samtalen hoppede fra det ene trivielle emne til det næste og gik flere gange i stå. Han blev så længe, at fyrstinde Marja og Natasja vekslede blikke. De spekulerede åbenbart på, hvornår han gik. Pierre så det, men kunne ikke gå. Han sad ilde til mode og pinligt berørt, men blev siddende, for han kunne simpelthen ikke rejse sig og sige farvel.
Fyrstinde Marja, der ikke så nogen ende, rejste sig først og klagede over hovedpine, mens hun begyndte at sige godnat.
»Så De rejser til Petersborg i morgen?« spurgte hun.

»Nej, det gør jeg ikke,« svarede Pierre hastigt i en overrasket tone, som om han var fornærmet. »Jo... nej... til Petersborg? I morgen — men jeg siger ikke farvel endnu. Jeg kigger forbi i tilfælde af, at De har nogen ærinder for mig,« sagde han og stod foran fyrstinde Marja med rødmende ansigt uden at tage sin afsked.

Natasja rakte ham hånden og gik. Fyrstinde Marja derimod, i stedet for at gå, sank ned i en lænestol og betragtede ham strengt og indtrængende med sine dybe, strålende øjne. Den træthed, hun havde vist lige før, var nu helt forsvundet. Med et dybt og langtrukket suk så det ud, som om hun forberedte sig på en lang samtale.
Da Natasja havde forladt rummet, forsvandt Pierres forvirring og akavethed øjeblikkeligt og blev erstattet af ivrig ophidselse. Han rykkede hurtigt en lænestol hen mod fyrstinde Marja.

»Ja, jeg ville sige Dem,« sagde han og svarede på hendes blik, som om hun havde talt. »Fyrstinde, hjælp mig! Hvad skal jeg gøre? Tør jeg håbe? Fyrstinde, min kære veninde, hør mig! Jeg ved det alt sammen. Jeg ved, at jeg er hende uværdig, jeg ved, at det er umuligt at tale om det nu. Men jeg vil være en bror for hende. Nej, ikke det, jeg... jeg kan ikke...«
Han standsede og gned sit ansigt og sine øjne med hænderne.

»Nå,« fortsatte han med en tydelig anstrengelse for at beherske sig og tale sammenhængende. »Jeg ved ikke, hvornår jeg begyndte at elske hende, men jeg har elsket hende og hende alene hele mit liv, og jeg elsker hende sådan, at jeg ikke kan forestille mig livet uden hende. Jeg kan ikke fri til hende nu, men tanken om, at hun måske en dag kunne blive min kone, og at jeg går glip af den mulighed... den mulighed... er forfærdelig. Sig mig, er der håb? Sig mig, hvad jeg skal gøre? Kære fyrstinde!« sagde han efter en kort pause og rørte ved hendes hånd, da hun ikke svarede.
»Jeg tænker over det, De har fortalt mig,« svarede fyrstinde Marja. »Her er, hvad jeg vil sige. De har ret i, at det at tale til hende om kærlighed nu...«

Fyrstinde Marja standsede. Hun havde været ved at sige, at det ville være umuligt at tale om kærlighed, men hun holdt inde, fordi hun af den pludselige forandring i Natasja to dage forinden havde set, at hun ikke blot ikke ville blive såret, hvis Pierre talte om sin kærlighed, men at det var netop det, hun ønskede.
»At tale til hende nu ville ikke gå,« sagde fyrstinden alligevel.
»Men hvad skal jeg gøre?«
»Overlad det til mig,« sagde fyrstinde Marja. »Jeg ved...«
Pierre så ind i fyrstinde Marjas øjne.
»Nå?... Nå?...« sagde han.
»Jeg ved, at hun elsker... vil elske Dem,« rettede fyrstinde Marja sig.
Før hun havde talt færdigt, var Pierre sprunget op og havde med et forskrækket udtryk grebet fyrstinde Marjas hånd.
»Hvad får Dem til at tro det? Tror De, jeg tør håbe? Tror De...?«

»Ja, det tror jeg,« sagde fyrstinde Marja med et smil. »Skriv til hendes forældre, og overlad resten til mig. Jeg fortæller hende det, når tiden er inde. Jeg ønsker det, og mit hjerte siger mig, at det vil ske.«
»Nej, det kan ikke være! Hvor er jeg lykkelig! Men det kan ikke være... Hvor er jeg lykkelig! Nej, det kan ikke være!« blev Pierre ved med at sige, mens han kyssede fyrstinde Marjas hænder.
»Tag til Petersborg, det er det bedste. Og jeg skriver til Dem,« sagde hun.
»Til Petersborg? Tage derhen? Godt, jeg tager. Men må jeg komme igen i morgen?«

Næste dag kom Pierre for at sige farvel. Natasja var mindre livlig end dagen før; men den dag, når han så på hende, følte Pierre somme tider, som om han forsvandt, og at hverken han eller hun eksisterede længere, at intet eksisterede undtagen lykke. »Er det muligt? Nej, det kan ikke være,« sagde han til sig selv ved hvert blik på hende, hvert smil, hver forandring i hendes ansigt.
Da han ved afskeden tog hendes tynde, slanke hånd, kunne han ikke lade være med at holde den en smule længere i sin egen.

»Er det muligt, at denne hånd, dette ansigt, disse øjne, hele denne skat af kvindelig ynde, som er mig så fremmed nu — er det muligt, at alt dette en dag vil blive mit for altid, lige så velkendt for mig, som jeg er for mig selv?... Nej, det er umuligt!...«
»Farvel, greve,« sagde hun højt. »Jeg skal se meget frem til Deres tilbagekomst,« tilføjede hun hviskende.

Og disse enkle ord, hendes blik og det udtryk i hendes ansigt, der ledsagede dem, udgjorde i to måneder emnet for uudtømmelige minder, fortolkninger og lykkelige tanker for Pierre. »'Jeg skal se meget frem til Deres tilbagekomst...' Ja, ja, hvordan sagde hun det? Ja: 'Jeg skal se meget frem til Deres tilbagekomst.' Å, hvor er jeg lykkelig! Hvad sker der med mig? Hvor er jeg lykkelig!« sagde Pierre til sig selv.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, now frowning over a difficult problem, now suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, now smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that feeling. It was already six in the morning and he still paced the room.

"Well, what's to be done if there's no way around it? What can I do? Obviously this is how it has to be," he told himself, and hastily undressing, he got into bed—happy and agitated, but free of hesitation or indecision.
"Strange and impossible as such happiness seems, I must do everything I can so that she and I may become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke on Thursday, Savelich came to ask about packing for the trip.

"What—Petersburg? What is Petersburg? Who's in Petersburg?" he asked, though only of himself. "Oh yes, a long time ago—before all this happened—I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he reflected. "Why? But maybe I will go. What a good, considerate fellow he is!" he thought, looking at Savelich. "And what a nice smile!"
"Well, Savelich, do you still not want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never been mistreated."
"And your children?"
"The children will be fine just the same. With masters like you, anyone can get along."
"But what about my heirs?" said Pierre. "Suppose I suddenly get married... it could happen," he added with an involuntary smile.
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a very good thing."
"He thinks it's so easy," Pierre thought. "He doesn't know how terrifying it is, how dangerous. Too soon or too late... it's terrifying!"
"So what are your orders? Are you leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.

"No, I'll put it off a bit. I'll tell you later. Forgive me for the trouble I've put you through," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "How strange it is that he doesn't know there is no Petersburg for me now, and that this has to be settled first. But he probably does know and is just pretending. Should I talk to him about it? No, some other time."
At breakfast, Pierre told the princess—his cousin—that he'd been to see Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to find this no more remarkable than if he'd seen some Anna Semyonovna.
"Do you know her?" Pierre asked.
"I've seen the princess," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. That would be very good for the Rostovs—they're said to be completely ruined."
"No—I mean, do you know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was very unfortunate."
"She either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything to her either."
The princess had also prepared provisions for Pierre's journey.
"How kind they all are," Pierre thought. "What's amazing is that they bother with these things now, when none of it could matter to them anymore. And all for me!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to Pierre, inviting him to send a representative to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was being returned to its owners.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine, good-looking officer, and how kind. Think of him bothering with such trifles right now! And people actually say he's dishonest and takes bribes. What nonsense! And besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised. Everyone does it. But what a pleasant, kind face, and how he smiles as he looks at me!"
Pierre went to Princess Mary's for dinner.

As he drove through the streets past burned-out houses, he was struck by the beauty of those ruins. The chimney stacks and crumbling walls, stretching out to conceal one another, reminded him of the Rhine and the Colosseum. The cab drivers and passengers he passed, the carpenters working on frames for new buildings, the women selling goods at the street corners—all looked at him with cheerful, beaming faces that seemed to say: "Ah, here he is! Let's see what comes of this!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house, Pierre felt unsure whether he had really been there the night before, really seen Natasha and talked with her. "Maybe I imagined it. Maybe I'll go in and find no one." But he had barely entered the room when he felt her presence—felt it through the sudden loss of his freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with soft folds, and her hair was arranged the same way as the evening before, but she was completely different. If she had looked like this the night before when he entered the room, he couldn't have failed to recognize her for a single instant.
She was as he had known her almost as a child and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly and strangely playful expression.
Pierre stayed for dinner and would have spent the whole evening there, but Princess Mary was going to vespers and Pierre left with her.

The next day he came early, stayed for dinner, and spent the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked over everything and the conversation kept moving between those insignificant topics that arise when people want to keep talking but can't find new subjects. Pierre stayed so late that Princess Mary and Natasha kept exchanging glances, obviously waiting for him to leave. Pierre saw this but couldn't bring himself to go. He felt heavy and awkward, but still sat on because he simply couldn't get up and leave.
Princess Mary, foreseeing no end to it, was the first to rise and, complaining of a headache, began to say good night.
"So you're going to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre replied hastily, in a surprised, almost offended tone. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing before Princess Mary, flushing and fidgeting, not leaving.

Natasha gave him her hand and left the room. Princess Mary, instead of going, sank into an armchair and fixed her deep, radiant eyes on him with a look that was both stern and intent. The weariness she'd plainly shown before had completely vanished. With a deep, heavy sigh she seemed to be preparing herself for a long conversation.
The instant Natasha left, Pierre's awkwardness and confusion disappeared and were replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled a chair up to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, responding to her look as if she had spoken. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to talk about it now. But I want to be her brother. No, I don't... I can't..."
He paused and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, clearly struggling for self-control and coherence. "I don't know when I first began to love her, but I've loved her and her alone all my life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't ask for her hand right now, but the thought that maybe she could be mine, and that I might miss that chance... that chance... is terrible. Tell me—can I hope? Tell me, what should I do? Dear princess!" he said after a brief pause, touching her hand when she didn't reply.
"I'm thinking about what you've told me," Princess Mary answered. "This is what I'll say. You're right that to speak to her of love at present—"

Princess Mary stopped. She'd been about to say that speaking of love was impossible, but she stopped because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days ago that Natasha would not only not be hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, but that it was the one thing she wanted.
"To speak to her now wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what am I to do?"
"Leave it to me," said Princess Mary. "I know..."
Pierre was looking into Princess Mary's eyes.
"Well?... Well?..." he said.
"I know that she loves... will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before the words were out, Pierre had sprung up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a frightened expression.
"What makes you think so? You think I can hope? You think—?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary with a smile. "Write to her parents, and leave it to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want this to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept saying as he kissed Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that would be best. And I'll write to you," she said.
"To Petersburg? Go there? Very well, I'll go. But may I come again tomorrow?"

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than the day before; but as he looked at her, Pierre sometimes felt as if he were vanishing, as if neither he nor she existed anymore, that nothing existed but happiness. "Can this be real? No, it can't," he told himself at every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his heart with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer in his.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, those eyes—all this treasure of feminine charm, so strange to me now—is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar as I am to myself?... No, that's impossible!"
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll very much look forward to your return," she added in a whisper.

And these simple words, her look, and the expression on her face that accompanied them formed, for two months, the subject of inexhaustible memories, interpretations, and happy meditations for Pierre. "'I'll very much look forward to your return.' How did she say it? How did she look? What did she mean? What was the look in her eyes?" And his recalled impression was so vivid that it seemed to happen right then, and he would smile all over again.
